script.opening: "I’m about nine weeks pregnant and I just can’t stop being sick — I can’t keep food down, and now not even water; it comes straight back up. I’m exhausted, dizzy when I stand, I’ve barely passed urine today, and I’ve lost weight. Everyone says it’s just morning sickness but this feels really wrong and I’m frightened for the baby."

facts.text: Started at 6 weeks, much worse over the last week. Nauseous all day, "every hour of the day". Vomiting more than 5 times a day and retching constantly. Nothing has stayed down since last night, not even sips of water.

Passed urine once this morning — small and dark. Dizzy when she stands; had to sit on the bathroom floor. Mouth very dry. Clothes loose — thinks she’s lost 3–4 kg (was 62 kg before pregnancy). Not confused.

No blood in the vomit. No tummy pain apart from aching muscles from retching. No fever. No diarrhoea. No burning or frequency when passing urine. No vaginal bleeding. No headaches or palpitations. No previous stomach problems.
First pregnancy, planned. Positive test at 4 weeks; dating scan not yet done (booked for next week). Hasn’t seen the midwife yet — booking appointment is next week.
Was taking folic acid but can’t keep it down. Has taken nothing for the sickness — "I was scared it would harm the baby." No allergies. No previous medical problems.

Low and exhausted, crying a lot, "I just want it to stop", but no thoughts of harming herself or ending the pregnancy if asked. Husband, Marco, works shifts but can drive her. Works in a bakery — the smells make it worse; off sick this week.

Weak, quiet, lying on the sofa with a sick bowl. Answer in short phrases. You feel dismissed by everyone saying "morning sickness". Feel listened to if the doctor takes it seriously. Ask: "Are the anti-sickness medicines safe for the baby?" Agree to go to hospital if it is explained.

ice.ideas: "This isn’t normal morning sickness. Something’s wrong."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — "That the baby isn’t getting anything and will be harmed. And that no one will listen." Her sister had a miscarriage last year.
ice.expectations: "For someone to take it seriously and stop the sickness — without anything that could hurt the baby."

cues: "Not even water" — the key point that decides same-day IV fluids.
"Everyone says it’s just morning sickness" — feeling dismissed.
"I was scared to take anything in case it harms the baby" — fear of medicines to address with safe options.

checkpoints.text: Distinguishes ordinary NVP from HYPEREMESIS GRAVIDARUM (RCOG GTG 69, 2024 — Windsor definition: onset before 16 weeks, severe nausea or vomiting, inability to eat and/or drink normally, strong limitation of daily activities, dehydration signs contributing) — not dismissing it as "morning sickness"

Assesses SEVERITY objectively — PUQE score, clinical dehydration signs (face to face, not on video), weight loss, ability to tolerate oral fluids, U&E — not ketonuria (RCOG 2024) — with the key discriminator being whether she can keep fluids down

Decides DISPOSITION correctly — inability to keep fluids or oral antiemetics down / clinical dehydration/electrolyte derangement → same-day referral for IV REHYDRATION (day unit/admission); milder cases managed in the community with review

Prescribes SAFE antiemetics in pregnancy (cyclizine/promethazine/prochlorperazine/chlorpromazine first-line; ondansetron second line, not discouraged (RCOG 2024; MHRA 2020); metoclopramide limited to 5 days (MHRA 2013)), ensures THIAMINE (100 mg three times daily orally or IV B complex if admitted), and considers LMWH/electrolyte replacement if admitted/dehydrated
Considers and excludes other causes/complications (UTI, molar/multiple pregnancy — ultrasound, thyroid dysfunction, other abdominal pathology; AKI, Wernicke’s)
Validates that this is a recognised, treatable condition (not "just morning sickness"), addresses her fear for the baby, asks about her mood, and supports her through a debilitating illness
Explains the plan and reasoning clearly, checks understanding, and reassures appropriately

Safety-nets and follows up: return/urgent if unable to keep fluids down, worsening dehydration, reduced urine, abdominal pain or feeling very unwell; arranges IV rehydration/referral as needed, antiemetic review, and follow-up — severity-based disposition + safe treatment, not dismissal

worked.txt: "You’re right that this isn’t ‘just morning sickness’ — when you can’t keep down even water, you’re passing little urine and losing weight, that’s a recognised condition called hyperemesis gravidarum, and it needs proper treatment. I’m glad you came."

"I can’t check how dehydrated you are over video — your pulse and blood pressure sitting and standing and your mouth need someone to see you in person, so the pregnancy day unit will do that today, with your weight and some bloods for your salts and kidneys. A urine dip for ‘ketones’ doesn’t tell us how dehydrated you are. The key question is whether you can hold any fluids down at all — when did you last keep a drink down?"

"Because you can’t keep fluids down and you’re dehydrated, the safest thing is to get you fluids into a vein — I’ll arrange that today, either at the day-assessment unit or hospital. That settles things much faster than trying to sip at home."

"There are anti-sickness medicines that are safe in pregnancy — the unit can give one like cyclizine by injection, as tablets won’t stay down — and they’ll give a vitamin (thiamine) to protect your brain and nerves during the sickness. If the first medicine doesn’t work, there are good second options. Treating this protects both you and the baby."

"I’ll also check there’s nothing else adding to it — a water infection, your thyroid — and a scan will confirm the pregnancy and check it’s not twins or anything unusual, which can make sickness worse."

"This is treatable and it does usually ease as pregnancy goes on. How has your mood been with all this? Please don’t drive yourself to the unit. Come back urgently — or to the unit — if you still can’t keep fluids down, you’re passing very little urine, get tummy pain, or feel really unwell. We’ll review you closely."

f.learning: Distinguish ordinary nausea/vomiting of pregnancy (NVP) from HYPEREMESIS GRAVIDARUM — RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 69 (2024), using the Windsor definition (international): onset before 16 weeks, nausea and vomiting with at least one severe, INABILITY to eat and/or drink normally and strong limitation of daily activities, with DEHYDRATION signs contributing (replacing the older triad of >5% weight loss, dehydration and electrolyte disturbance) — because inability to keep down even fluids, reduced urine output, light-headedness and weight loss mark a serious condition, not "just morning sickness". Assess severity objectively with the PUQE score, dehydration signs (tachycardia, postural drop, dry mucous membranes — assessed face to face, not on video — and reduced urine output), weight loss versus booking weight, the ability to tolerate oral fluids and antiemetics, and U&E (electrolytes/AKI) — not KETONURIA, which RCOG 2024 says is not an indicator of dehydration — the key practical discriminator being whether she can keep ORAL FLUIDS down. Decide DISPOSITION on severity: inability to tolerate fluids or oral antiemetics, clinical dehydration, abnormal electrolytes, or failure of community antiemetics warrants referral for IV REHYDRATION via an ambulatory/day-assessment unit or admission, whereas milder cases tolerating some fluids can be managed in the community with oral antiemetics and review — do not leave a woman who cannot tolerate fluids to "try ginger and crackers". Prescribe SAFE antiemetics in pregnancy (cyclizine, promethazine, prochlorperazine or chlorpromazine first-line, non-oral if tablets are not kept down; second line ondansetron, whose use RCOG 2024 says should not be discouraged if first line fails (MHRA January 2020: very small increase in absolute oral-cleft risk with first-trimester use), or metoclopramide limited to 5 days (MHRA August 2013)), give THIAMINE to prevent Wernicke’s encephalopathy (RCOG: oral 100 mg three times daily or IV vitamin B complex for all women admitted with vomiting or severely reduced intake), consider LMWH if admitted (RCOG GTG 37a), and replace electrolytes. Ask about mood and offer support (RCOG 2024). Consider and exclude other causes/complications: UTI, MOLAR or MULTIPLE pregnancy (ultrasound), THYROID dysfunction, and other abdominal pathology, alongside complications such as electrolyte disturbance, AKI and Wernicke’s. The hidden agenda is fear for the baby and feeling dismissed; validate that this is recognised and treatable, assess severity, arrange correct disposition (IV fluids if not tolerating oral), prescribe safe antiemetics and thiamine, exclude mimics, and follow up compassionately.

knowledge.guideline: [1] RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 69 The management of nausea and vomiting in pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum (February 2024) · [2] MHRA Drug Safety Update: ondansetron and oral clefts (January 2020) · [3] MHRA Drug Safety Update: metoclopramide and neurological adverse effects (August 2013) · [4] RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 37a Reducing the risk of venous thromboembolism during pregnancy and the puerperium (2015) · [5] BNF: antiemetics in pregnancy · [6] Windsor definition of hyperemesis gravidarum (2021) (international)
knowledge.summary: At 9 weeks she cannot keep down food or water, is passing little urine, feels faint on standing and has lost weight. This is hyperemesis gravidarum, not “morning sickness”. RCOG GTG 69 (2024) is symptom-based: severity is judged on PUQE, whether fluids and oral antiemetics stay down, and clinical dehydration, not on urine ketones. Because she cannot tolerate fluids and cannot be examined on video, she needs same-day ambulatory care or admission for IV fluids, parenteral antiemetics, thiamine and bloods, with a clear follow-up plan and support.

points.t: RCOG GTG 69 (2024) [1] uses the Windsor consensus definition [6] (international): onset before 16 weeks, nausea and vomiting with at least one severe, inability to eat and/or drink normally, and strong limitation of daily activities; signs of dehydration contribute. It replaced the older triad of more than 5% weight loss, dehydration and electrolyte imbalance.

RCOG [1]: use the PUQE score (three questions: hours of nausea, episodes of vomiting and of retching a day; mild 6 or less, moderate 7 to 12, severe 13 to 15) with a clinical assessment of hydration, weight and bloods (U&E). Ketonuria is not an indicator of dehydration and should not be used to judge severity.

RCOG [1]: mild NVP is managed in the community. Ambulatory day care gives IV fluids, vitamins (especially thiamine) and parenteral antiemetics, and should be used where possible. Admission is considered when symptoms are not controlled with ambulatory care, or when there are complications or comorbidity. Rehydrate with sodium chloride with potassium as needed, not dextrose.

RCOG [1]: first line are doxylamine/pyridoxine, antihistamines and phenothiazines such as cyclizine, promethazine, prochlorperazine and chlorpromazine (dose per BNF [5]). Second line: ondansetron, whose use should not be discouraged if first line fails; MHRA [2] noted a very small increase in the absolute risk of oral clefts with first-trimester use, to be balanced against poorly managed HG. Metoclopramide is second line, limited to 5 days because of extrapyramidal effects (MHRA [3]). Use a non-oral route if tablets are not kept down.

RCOG [1]: give thiamine (oral 100 mg three times daily or IV as part of vitamin B complex) to all women admitted with vomiting or severely reduced intake, especially before dextrose or parenteral nutrition, to prevent Wernicke’s encephalopathy. RCOG GTG 37a [4]: hyperemesis is a transient VTE risk factor; consider LMWH during admission.

Onset later than usual in pregnancy, abdominal pain, fever, headache or diarrhoea suggest another cause. Check urine for infection, U&E, LFTs and TFTs if severe, and an ultrasound to confirm viability and exclude multiple or molar pregnancy. RCOG [1]: assess mental health, offer support (including charity support), and do not recommend ginger for HG. In a future pregnancy, offer pre-emptive advice and early treatment.

Idea (more than morning sickness), concern (the baby; not being listened to), expectation (help today).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — "That the baby isn’t getting anything and will be harmed. And that no one will listen." Her sister had a miscarriage last year — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mrs Marenco, I’m Dr Rahman. Can you hear and see me clearly? And can I check where you are right now, in case I need to arrange anything?
model.why: Video set-up and location for urgent action

model.text: Yes, I’m at home.
Thank you. Tell me what’s been happening.

I’m about nine weeks pregnant and I just can’t stop being sick. I can’t keep food down, and now not even water; it comes straight back up. I’m exhausted, dizzy when I stand, I’ve barely passed urine today, and I’ve lost weight. Everyone says it’s just morning sickness but this feels really wrong and I’m frightened for the baby.
You’re right to take this seriously, and I’m glad you called. Let me ask some quick questions so we can get you the right help today.
Roughly how many hours a day do you feel sick, how many times a day are you vomiting, and how often are you retching?
Nauseous all day. Sick more than five times. Retching constantly.
When did you last keep a drink down? And when did you last pass urine?
Nothing’s stayed down since last night. Once this morning, dark.
Do you know how much weight you’ve lost?
My clothes are loose. I think a few kilos.
Any blood in the vomit, tummy pain, fever, pain passing urine, diarrhoea or headache?
No blood. My stomach aches from being sick, that’s all. No fever.
Any vaginal bleeding? And have you had a scan yet in this pregnancy?
model.why: Early pregnancy problems; molar or multiple pregnancy

model.text: No bleeding. I haven’t had a scan yet.
Any confusion, double vision or unsteadiness beyond the dizziness when you stand?
No, just dizzy and weak.
Have you tried any anti-sickness medicine? Any allergies?
Nothing. I was scared to take anything in case it harms the baby. No allergies.
You said you’re frightened for the baby. What worries you most?
That the baby isn’t getting anything. And that no one will listen.
That’s a very understandable fear. How are you coping in yourself? Some women find this so hard that their mood really drops.
I’m low and exhausted. I just want it to stop.

This isn’t ordinary morning sickness. It’s a condition called hyperemesis gravidarum, a severe form of pregnancy sickness. It’s recognised and treatable. Because you can’t keep even water down and you’re dizzy and passing little urine, you’re dehydrated, and I can’t check your blood pressure or pulse over video.
model.why: Names HG; explains reasoning and the video limit

model.text: On the baby: in early pregnancy the baby is well protected, and treating you properly is the best thing for both of you.
model.why: Addresses fear for the baby honestly

model.text: So what happens now?

I’d like you seen today at the hospital’s pregnancy day unit. They’ll check your pulse and blood pressure, do blood tests for your salts and kidneys, check your urine for infection, and give you a drip of fluids with anti-sickness medicine and a vitamin called thiamine through the vein. Many women go home the same day feeling much better. They can also arrange a scan to check the pregnancy.
model.why: Same-day ambulatory care: IV fluids, parenteral antiemetic, thiamine, bloods, scan (RCOG GTG 69)

model.text: Are the anti-sickness medicines safe?

Yes. The first-choice ones, like cyclizine or prochlorperazine, have been used in pregnancy for many years. You’ll go home with regular tablets, and there are other options if they don’t work. Leaving this untreated is the bigger risk.
model.why: Safe first-line antiemetics; counsels on safety

model.text: I’ll phone the unit now and send them my notes. Please don’t drive yourself while you’re dizzy. Is there someone who can take you?
Yes, I can get someone to take me.
Can you tell me what you’re going to do next?
Go to the pregnancy unit today for a drip, blood tests and a scan.

That’s it. If you faint, become confused, see double, vomit blood, get severe tummy pain or bleeding before you get there, call 999. I’ll call you after you’ve been seen, and we’ll keep reviewing you, with a fit note if you need one. You won’t be told to just put up with this.

social.t: Many women with HG are told it is normal morning sickness. Naming the condition and acting on it rebuilds trust.
Childcare, transport and help at home matter while she is unwell. Ask who can support her.

legal.t: Offer a fit note. Pregnancy-related sickness absence is protected: under the Equality Act 2010, unfavourable treatment because of pregnancy-related illness is unlawful.
She should not drive while dizzy and dehydrated.

professional.t: Hydration and observations cannot be assessed on video. When the decision depends on them, arrange same-day face-to-face assessment.
Phone the unit and send a summary: gestation, PUQE answers, oral intolerance, urine output, no antiemetics so far, allergy status.

community.t: Ensure she is booked with a midwife. Pregnancy sickness charities offer peer support. Screen mood at each contact, and plan early treatment in any future pregnancy.

redFlags: Unable to keep fluids or oral antiemetics down
Abdominal pain, fever or urinary symptoms (mimics)
Low mood or thoughts of ending the pregnancy or her life
ice: Concern: the baby is not getting anything; no one will listen

playbook.diagnosis: “This is hyperemesis gravidarum, a severe form of pregnancy sickness. You’re dehydrated and need fluids and treatment today.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Pregnancy hormones cause sickness in most women, but in a few it becomes so severe that they can’t eat or drink. It’s not your fault and it’s treatable.”

management.reflectIce: “You were right that this isn’t ordinary morning sickness, and getting you treated is the best thing for you and the baby.”
management.psychosocial: Validate; address fear of medicines; screen mood; arrange transport; offer a fit note.
sharedPlan: Same-day pregnancy day unit: IV fluids, parenteral antiemetic, thiamine (RCOG GTG 69, 2024)
Bloods (U&E, and LFTs and TFTs if severe), urine culture, weight, ultrasound for viability and number
Regular first-line antiemetic on discharge; second-line options if needed (MHRA January 2020; August 2013)
safetyNet: Fainting, confusion, double vision, haematemesis, severe pain or bleeding: 999
GP call after unit assessment; ongoing review
Return the same day if unable to keep fluids or tablets down again

pitfalls.intro: The trap is the label “morning sickness”. This station tests whether the candidate recognises that a woman who cannot keep water down needs fluids today, and whether they can do so warmly over video.

items.fail: Managing at home with an oral antiemetic.
items.why: She cannot keep fluids down; RCOG GTG 69 uses ambulatory IV rehydration for this.
items.fix: Arrange same-day assessment at the pregnancy day unit.

items.fail: Using urine ketones to judge severity.
items.why: RCOG 2024: ketonuria is not an indicator of dehydration.
items.fix: Use PUQE, oral tolerance, clinical hydration and U&E.
Make sure thiamine is given, and ask about confusion and eye symptoms.

items.fail: Not considering mimics or molar or multiple pregnancy.
items.why: UTI, surgical causes and molar pregnancy can present this way; she has not had a scan.
items.fix: Ask about pain, fever and bleeding; request urine culture and ultrasound.

items.fail: Reassuring about the baby without hearing her fear.
items.fix: Ask what worries her most, then answer honestly.

items.fail: No safety-net for the journey or follow-up after the unit.
items.why: She is dizzy and dehydrated, and HG often recurs after discharge.
items.fix: Give 999 red flags, advise not driving, and book a follow-up call.

avoid.dont: “Try ginger biscuits and small sips of water.”
avoid.instead: “You can’t keep water down, so you need fluids through a drip today.”
avoid.why: RCOG GTG 69 (2024) advises against ginger for HG, and she cannot tolerate oral intake.

avoid.dont: “Check your urine for ketones to see how dehydrated you are.”
avoid.instead: “The unit will check your pulse, blood pressure and blood salts.”
avoid.why: RCOG 2024: ketonuria is not an indicator of dehydration and should not be used to assess severity.

avoid.dont: “It’s best to avoid medicines in pregnancy.”
avoid.instead: “The first-choice anti-sickness medicines have long safety records in pregnancy.”
avoid.why: Undertreatment harms mother and pregnancy; first-line antiemetics are recommended (RCOG GTG 69).

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 69 The management of nausea and vomiting in pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum (February 2024) · [2] MHRA Drug Safety Update: ondansetron and oral clefts (January 2020) · [3] MHRA Drug Safety Update: metoclopramide and neurological adverse effects (August 2013) · [4] RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 37a Reducing the risk of venous thromboembolism during pregnancy and the puerperium (2015) · [5] BNF: antiemetics in pregnancy · [6] Windsor definition of hyperemesis gravidarum (2021) (international)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: At 9 weeks she cannot keep down food or water, is passing little urine, feels faint on standing and has lost weight. This is hyperemesis gravidarum, not “morning sickness”. RCOG GTG 69 (2024) is symptom-based: severity is judged on PUQE, whether fluids and oral antiemetics stay down, and clinical dehydration, not on urine ketones. Because she cannot tolerate fluids and cannot be examined on video, she needs same-day ambulatory care or admission for IV fluids, parenteral antiemetics, thiamine and bloods, with a clear follow-up plan and support.

points.t: RCOG GTG 69 (2024) [1] uses the Windsor consensus definition [6] (international): onset before 16 weeks, nausea and vomiting with at least one severe, inability to eat and/or drink normally, and strong limitation of daily activities; signs of dehydration contribute. It replaced the older triad of more than 5% weight loss, dehydration and electrolyte imbalance.

RCOG [1]: use the PUQE score (three questions: hours of nausea, episodes of vomiting and of retching a day; mild 6 or less, moderate 7 to 12, severe 13 to 15) with a clinical assessment of hydration, weight and bloods (U&E). Ketonuria is not an indicator of dehydration and should not be used to judge severity.

RCOG [1]: mild NVP is managed in the community. Ambulatory day care gives IV fluids, vitamins (especially thiamine) and parenteral antiemetics, and should be used where possible. Admission is considered when symptoms are not controlled with ambulatory care, or when there are complications or comorbidity. Rehydrate with sodium chloride with potassium as needed, not dextrose.

RCOG [1]: first line are doxylamine/pyridoxine, antihistamines and phenothiazines such as cyclizine, promethazine, prochlorperazine and chlorpromazine (dose per BNF [5]). Second line: ondansetron, whose use should not be discouraged if first line fails; MHRA [2] noted a very small increase in the absolute risk of oral clefts with first-trimester use, to be balanced against poorly managed HG. Metoclopramide is second line, limited to 5 days because of extrapyramidal effects (MHRA [3]). Use a non-oral route if tablets are not kept down.

RCOG [1]: give thiamine (oral 100 mg three times daily or IV as part of vitamin B complex) to all women admitted with vomiting or severely reduced intake, especially before dextrose or parenteral nutrition, to prevent Wernicke’s encephalopathy. RCOG GTG 37a [4]: hyperemesis is a transient VTE risk factor; consider LMWH during admission.

Onset later than usual in pregnancy, abdominal pain, fever, headache or diarrhoea suggest another cause. Check urine for infection, U&E, LFTs and TFTs if severe, and an ultrasound to confirm viability and exclude multiple or molar pregnancy. RCOG [1]: assess mental health, offer support (including charity support), and do not recommend ginger for HG. In a future pregnancy, offer pre-emptive advice and early treatment.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open start after confirming location for urgent action; acknowledged her distress.
Mood, exhaustion, fear for the baby and feeling dismissed explored; transport and support checked.
Picked up “not even water” and “barely passed urine” and assessed oral tolerance and output.
Idea (more than morning sickness), concern (the baby; not being listened to), expectation (help today).
Recognised that video cannot assess dehydration; same-day unit for observations, U&E, urine culture, weight and ultrasound.
HG versus UTI, gastroenteritis, molar or multiple pregnancy, thyroid and surgical causes.
Screened haematemesis, abdominal pain, fever, bleeding and Wernicke’s features.
Named hyperemesis gravidarum with severe PUQE and inability to tolerate fluids (RCOG GTG 69, 2024).
Same-day ambulatory care for IV fluids, parenteral antiemetics and thiamine; first-line antiemetics counselled as safe.
Low mood and fear of medicines addressed; fit note offered; safe travel arranged.
999 red flags given; call after assessment; ongoing review.

social.t: Many women with HG are told it is normal morning sickness. Naming the condition and acting on it rebuilds trust.
Childcare, transport and help at home matter while she is unwell. Ask who can support her.

legal.t: Offer a fit note. Pregnancy-related sickness absence is protected: under the Equality Act 2010, unfavourable treatment because of pregnancy-related illness is unlawful.
She should not drive while dizzy and dehydrated.

professional.t: Hydration and observations cannot be assessed on video. When the decision depends on them, arrange same-day face-to-face assessment.
Phone the unit and send a summary: gestation, PUQE answers, oral intolerance, urine output, no antiemetics so far, allergy status.

community.t: Ensure she is booked with a midwife. Pregnancy sickness charities offer peer support. Screen mood at each contact, and plan early treatment in any future pregnancy.

redFlags: Unable to keep fluids or oral antiemetics down
Abdominal pain, fever or urinary symptoms (mimics)
Low mood or thoughts of ending the pregnancy or her life
ice: Concern: the baby is not getting anything; no one will listen

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is hyperemesis gravidarum, a severe form of pregnancy sickness. You’re dehydrated and need fluids and treatment today.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Pregnancy hormones cause sickness in most women, but in a few it becomes so severe that they can’t eat or drink. It’s not your fault and it’s treatable.”

management.reflectIce: “You were right that this isn’t ordinary morning sickness, and getting you treated is the best thing for you and the baby.”
management.psychosocial: Validate; address fear of medicines; screen mood; arrange transport; offer a fit note.
sharedPlan: Same-day pregnancy day unit: IV fluids, parenteral antiemetic, thiamine (RCOG GTG 69, 2024)
Bloods (U&E, and LFTs and TFTs if severe), urine culture, weight, ultrasound for viability and number
Regular first-line antiemetic on discharge; second-line options if needed (MHRA January 2020; August 2013)
safetyNet: Fainting, confusion, double vision, haematemesis, severe pain or bleeding: 999
GP call after unit assessment; ongoing review
Return the same day if unable to keep fluids or tablets down again

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The trap is the label “morning sickness”. This station tests whether the candidate recognises that a woman who cannot keep water down needs fluids today, and whether they can do so warmly over video.

items.fail: Managing at home with an oral antiemetic.
items.why: She cannot keep fluids down; RCOG GTG 69 uses ambulatory IV rehydration for this.
items.fix: Arrange same-day assessment at the pregnancy day unit.

items.fail: Using urine ketones to judge severity.
items.why: RCOG 2024: ketonuria is not an indicator of dehydration.
items.fix: Use PUQE, oral tolerance, clinical hydration and U&E.
Make sure thiamine is given, and ask about confusion and eye symptoms.

items.fail: Not considering mimics or molar or multiple pregnancy.
items.why: UTI, surgical causes and molar pregnancy can present this way; she has not had a scan.
items.fix: Ask about pain, fever and bleeding; request urine culture and ultrasound.

items.fail: Reassuring about the baby without hearing her fear.
items.fix: Ask what worries her most, then answer honestly.

items.fail: No safety-net for the journey or follow-up after the unit.
items.why: She is dizzy and dehydrated, and HG often recurs after discharge.
items.fix: Give 999 red flags, advise not driving, and book a follow-up call.
